pr_title: Treat nil as 0 for optimistic locking.
pr_body:
### Summary

If the locking_column does not have a default value it is possible to
have records with a value of NULL for that column, whether because the
database exists from a time before rails defaulted the value saved to 0,
or because someone inserted values into the database directly.

This causes bogus `ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError`s as rails attempts
to update a record with a value of 0 in the locking_column, but the real
value is NULL.

### Other Information

I could no longer use `#_update_record` inside `#_update_row` as `#_update_record` uses an equality operator which does not do the right thing with the array passed to it.

Fixes #36264

issue_context.title: Optimistic locking does not handle nulls properly
issue_context.body:
This is related to https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/26024. https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/26050 fixes that bug partially but it is still broken in some cases.

When the column is null in the database, update succeeds when the `lock_version` is not specified by the user. When a `lock_version` of `0` is given, this should still succeed because `NULL` means the same as `0` in this case (first version) but the update fails.

The reason for this is that `previous_lock_value = read_attribute_before_type_cast(locking_column)` in https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/v5.1.7/activerecord/lib/active_record/locking/optimistic.rb#L83 returns `nil` when the user did not provide a `lock_version` but when the attribute is set, it returns that value.

### Steps to reproduce

```ruby
def test_lock_version_without_default_value_when_form_submit
  ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute("insert into posts(name) VALUES('Mark')")

  p1 = Post.find(1)
  p1.update(name: "Bob", lock_version: "0")
  p1.save
end
```

### Expected behavior

Record is updated 

### Actual behavior

A `ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError` is raised

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 5.1.7

**Ruby version**: 2.6.3
comments:
We can't apply the fix mentioned in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/26050#discussion_r75713005 despite it fixes your case, it will break a case when "lock_version" in database is `0`:
```ruby
  ActiveRecord::Base.connection.execute("insert into posts(name, lock_version) VALUES('Mark', '0')")

  p1 = Post.find(1)
  p1.update(name: "Bob", lock_version: "0")
  p1.save
```

Probably, Rails should generate query like
```sql
UPDATE "posts" SET "title" = "Bob", "updated_at" = "2019-07-27 15:34:12.150557", "lock_version" = 1 WHERE "posts"."id" = 1 AND ("posts"."lock_version" IS NULL OR "posts"."lock_version" = "0")
```
in those both cases.

Yes, we actually have this in our code right now to do that:

```ruby
# Patched because when `lock_version` is read as `0`, it may actually be `NULL` in the DB.
possible_previous_lock_value = previous_lock_value.to_i == 0 ? [nil, 0] : previous_lock_value

affected_rows = self.class.unscoped.where(
  locking_column => possible_previous_lock_value,
  self.class.primary_key => id_in_database
).update_all(
  attributes_with_values_for_update(attribute_names)
)
```

We couldn't use `_update_record` because it doesn't work with array values since it uses `attr.eq` in https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/0196551e6039ca864d1eee1e01819fcae12c1dc9/activerecord/lib/active_record/persistence.rb#L379

This issue has been automatically marked as stale because it has not been commented on for at least three months.
The resources of the Rails team are limited, and so we are asking for your help.
If you can still reproduce this error on the `6-0-stable` branch or on `master`, please reply with all of the information you have about it in order to keep the issue open.
Thank you for all your contributions.

review_comments:
By internal design, we should use `_update_record` here. I guess we should make `_update_record` understand how to build constraint from an array value:
```ruby
self.class._update_record(
locking_column => [nil, 0] # ("lock_version" IS NULL OR "lock_version" = "0")
...
)
```

/cc @kamipo

Would you suggest adding a case to `_update_record` (and the `_delete_record` method) to deal with this? Something like:

```
        constraints = _substitute_values(constraints).map do |attr, bind|
          if bind.is_a?(Enumerable)
            bind.map { |bind_value| attr.eq(bind_value) }.reduce(&:or)
          else
            attr.eq(bind)
          end
        end
```

though this would also require changing `_subtitute_values` to something like

```
            bind = if value.is_a?(Enumerable)
              value.map { |single_value| predicate_builder.build_bind_attribute(name, single_value) }
            else
              predicate_builder.build_bind_attribute(name, value)
            end
```

WDYT?

Ah, we could actually use the `ActiveRecord::PredicateBuilder::ArrayHandler` in the `_(update|delete)_record` methods like so (but would still need to change `_substitute_values` as above):

```
        constraints = _substitute_values(constraints).map do |attr, bind|
          if bind.is_a?(Enumerable)
            ActiveRecord::PredicateBuilder::ArrayHandler.new(predicate_builder).call(attr, bind)
          else
            attr.eq(bind)
          end
        end
```
Is there a reason why the predicate is being built directly inside `_(update|delete)_record` btw? Why isn't `predicate_builder#build` used?
@bogdanvlviv sorry to ping you again, just wondering if you had any insights from my questions above?

First of all, I want to apologize for the unclear first comment. By "By internal design, we should use _update_record here." I meant that it would be great to retain using `_update_record` for consistency, also using this method should get better performance(bbae710a405ce92074c1666dcf859196c29e2ed2) since it looks like in this case we prevent building AR-relation.

I've spent some time looking at this, but unfortunately, I haven't got any good answers to your questions yet.

Actually, I am fine with this implementation since it eliminates the issue. I just want to know @kamipo's thoughts about it. Related to fa779b380e61381a393afbc7bbc0a9ce07e0ce74
Sorry to be a bother - it's been quite a bit (over a month now 😅) and was wondering if we could maybe get someone else's thoughts about it instead, since @kamipo seems to be quite busy?
`"posts"."lock_version" IS NULL OR "posts"."lock_version" = "0"` is redundant, it should just be to be `"posts"."lock_version" IS NULL` if `lock_version` was nil.

@kamipo thanks for taking a look! The problem is that we cannot know if `lock_version` was `nil` or `0` - it's unknown to us.

`previous_lock_value = read_attribute_before_type_cast(locking_column)` will hold a `0` even if the lock version is `nil`

so because of that, we must use `"posts"."lock_version" IS NULL OR "posts"."lock_version" = "0"` as we can't know what the actual value is in the DB

I could of course be missing something, could you please expand on your comment @kamipo ?
sorry for pinging yet again @kamipo -  I left some comments here on why we can't really do what you're suggesting. Could you please take a look?
